cells.tense: You're keeping the exchanges even right now, in real time, without having to stop and calculate.
cells.ask: Take one exchange you're already in, say out loud what each side gave, then leave it — no evening up, no extra sentence. Seeing it plainly, once, keeps the balance yours instead of automatic.
cells.core:
You can tell when something has tipped, yours or theirs, and you fix it early while it's still cheap to fix. The people across from you feel that evenness and rarely see the work in it. Nothing runs long enough to need a correction, because you're reading the small movements as they happen. An even exchange, in your hands, has a plain look to it: both sides get what they came for and neither has to keep watch afterward.

Reading the daily balances as they happen is what keeps this going. One exchange that's already settled can show you how you settled it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the exchanges even, and you do it in the moment.
cells.verb: Weigh what each exchange is actually giving and taking, then set it back to level

cells.tense: You're bracing for the moment the scales tip against you and getting there a step ahead of it.
cells.ask: Find one relationship you've been running a tally on and say the tally out loud to that person, even if it's small and even if you end up owing. Naming the real balance, once, ends the built-up position and trades it for contact.
cells.core:
The accounts are getting closed here before they're opened. You know each side's contributions down to the small ones, you know who owes what, and you're already braced for the moment it's taken from you. The running total is accurate; it's also doing the talking in rooms where the friendship used to. People close to you can feel they're sitting across from a ledger with the count already settled.

What you're protecting yourself from is not knowing whether you'll be treated fairly until it happens. A scale that's tipped is easier to face than one you're not allowed to watch. Here the pattern can't complete itself without an actual exchange.

cells.tense: There's a claim you never asked to be honored, and it's still open in front of you.
cells.ask: Write down what you're actually owed in one current situation — money, time, credit, an apology — and pick one item to ask for this week. The ask builds on what you already see; the question is what the asking puts back in your hands.
cells.core:
You can see how an exchange is supposed to run, where the balance belongs, what's fair without counting. And that's why the other half is thin: seeing the shape of a fair trade is not the same as standing in one, and the difference has gotten expensive. What's left is doing the watching instead of the exchanging, in a place where giving more than you get has become easier to carry than to name.

What's missing isn't the ability to see what's fair. It's the willingness to be someone with an end in the exchange. The claim doesn't need to be large; it needs to be made. You've put in steady effort before; this is the practice that gives it back.

cells.tense: You're keeping a tally here without having told yourself you're the one keeping it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been carrying as owed, in a single sentence, to yourself or to the person — just so the count becomes something you can see. Saying it out loud turns a pattern into a position, and a position can be acted on.
cells.core:
Small imbalances register, credits and debits land, and you usually know who's ahead before the exchange is over. What's missing is knowing that you are the one reading the scales. It feels like fairness lives in the situation and not in your hands, and the discrepancy keeps showing up without the fact that you're the one catching it. What the person across from you receives is the distance, not the arithmetic.

The instrument is accurate. The hand on it hasn't claimed itself. Naming one thing that's owed, even a small settled fact, hands the reading back to whoever is actually doing it — a shorter, earlier version of what's already running.
cells.sheetLine: You're already weighing it. You just haven't told yourself you are.

attempts.check: The unsupported claims here are the ones I avoided: I do not know this person has ever been cheated, discounted, drained, or has anyone tallying against them, and I do not know they have a practice, a room, or a conversation coming. The reader could say 'nothing has gone missing at my end — I never gave much' or 'I know exactly what I owe and I've said so'; either way the asks survive, because measuring this week's giving and receiving is useful even if nothing is off, and having one conversation about terms is useful even if they've had it before. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader would be any line that flatters the seat's cool pattern-reading into a gift — 'you see what everyone else misses' — so I left it out.
